t: How Failure Can Be Good For Your Students
q: Failure teaches us more than our successes. It reveals our mistakes and areas needing improvement.
Rarely are they required to face the plain, hard truth that they fell short.
When you give chance after chance after chance, happily accepting just about anything and everything, no matter how below par, you remove the intrinsic motivation to do better next time.
This underscores the critical importance of setting your students up for success before assigning graded work.

And if they don’t, if they choose to give a poor effort, if they turn in sub-par work or complete a test without care, if they don’t meet the standard you’ve set for them, then give them exactly what they’ve earned.
Stick to your guns. Be a teacher of integrity. Allow your students to learn the hard but life-changing lessons now, when they still have time.
As long as you provide every student the opportunity to succeed, the prospect of failure is one of the keys to creating a tenaciously motivated class.

t: Things I Believe about Grading Systems
q: Long-term flourishing isn't the A of the ABCs of teaching and education — it's the whole alphabet.

Every system I have seen people advocate for has its issues — anyone who tells you otherwise is either selling something or drinking the Kool-Aid. No matter what system you use, there are going to be benefits, and there are going to be problems.

Anyone telling you that one grading system is bad for all kids is overstating their case. Public education is still an experiment — and not all that old of an experiment by world historical standards.
If the perfect grading system requires teachers to spend unsustainable chunks of their time assessing or inputting or Managing the Machine, then it's not a perfect system.

Parents, too, need to understand the system. The better I am at communicating how grading works in my course — through the syllabus, through conferences, through the occasional email newsletter — the better the chances that parents will do their part to support their child in succeeding

t: How To Get Difficult Students To Listen To You https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/02/18/how-to-get-difficult-students-to-listen-to-you/
q: What you need is influence. Influence is that missing ingredient that will make your words matter and affect lasting change in behavior.
Every time you lecture, scold, threaten, argue with, or glare at difficult students you sabotage your influence with them.
But this communicates loud and clear that you can’t be trusted. It tells them that when you say something, it may or may not be true.
To build trust, and ultimately influence, you must be consistent day after day after day. You must follow your classroom management plan precisely as it’s written.

Extending simple kindness to your most difficult students, without manipulation, flattery, or expectation of receiving anything in return, has an almost magical way of unlocking powerful and influential rapport.
They appreciate this no-strings-attached interaction so much that despite themselves they’ll like and respect you.
They’ll stay with them and echo in their mind. Often for a lifetime.

q: Grading is not fun. I do not like grading. Therefore, my goal in grading is always this: do it as efficiently as possible.
But in order for me to understand whether I'm efficient or not, I have to know what the point of grading this particular assignment is.
When I give feedback on an AoW, it's at the whole-class or small-group level — hardly ever the individual level — because skill-building isn't the top priority.

t: Better and Saner Grading Tip: Stop “Relaxing” While Grading
q: But here is the problem: grading and/or giving feedback on student writing is active, mental work. Trying to grade while watching Netflix is akin to trying to jog while visually reading a book.
So you're sitting here, forcing your brain to try constantly switching between engaging with the show or engaging with the grading task.

After an hour of this, you end up, again, with probably much less enjoyment from the show and much less productivity with the grading than you could have gotten by giving an exclusive 30 minutes to each.
The literature is clear on this point. Engaging in any mentally challenging task should be done on its own — not while also watching television or carrying on a conversation.

At best, they decrease the quality of our evenings and increase the amount of time it takes to complete tasks. At worst, I wouldn't be surprised if we're damaging our brains, decreasing our ability over time to deeply engage with mentally challenging work for periods of, say, 60 minutes at a time.
When it's time to relax, relax. - When it's time to be done working, be done working.

t: Better and Saner Grading Tip: Get Out the Stopwatch
q: I don't have all the answers when it comes to taming the beast that is grading student writing, but here's something that I have found to help this year: using a stopwatch.
Step Three: Start the stopwatch and grade an essay. Do whatever it is that you do when you grade this kind of essay. Make comments, mark things, write on the rubric, assign a percentage, etc.

Are any of the things you do during a grading lap unlikely to help your students become better writers? Might you experiment with satisficing those things (or skipping them altogether) in the next round of five papers so as to improve your pace?

Timing forces quicker decision-making. I can't dither about what to write or not write; I just have to move forward with the task of helping this writer (my Want to Do) and assigning a score (my Have to Do).
Timing pushes back the urge to cover a paper with comments and markings. Me acting as a professional copyeditor is, at the risk of overgeneralizing, a pointless waste of my time.
No more wondering, no more dreading — I just know that this will take three more hours because I have 45 more papers and each paper takes me an average of four minutes to grade.

t: A Trick To Staying Calm All Day Long
q: You become a volcano simmering under the surface. Staying outwardly calm becomes an act of willpower rather than what it should be: A reflection of how you feel on the inside.
Now, before school begins each morning, sit quietly with your list and visualize yourself handling those moments calmly and successfully.

A great way to finish your visualization is to conjure up an outrageously—even comically—stressful situation, like a troop of Howler monkeys swinging through your door and windows, and then watching yourself handling it with aplomb.
Visualization has been shown to be nearly as effective as actual practice. And because you’re able to do it over and over again in a short period of time, it’s remarkably efficient.
You'll find yourself naturally handling things with grace and poise. You'll feel more prepared and confident and less hesitant.
x: Actively trying hard to stay calm often creates more tension, since it turns something meant to be effortless into an act of willpower.
A few minutes of morning visualization, imagining oneself handling stressful moments with composure, works even in as little as thirty seconds.
Ending a visualization session with an exaggerated, even comically stressful scenario builds resilience through humor.
Visualization has been shown to be nearly as effective as actual practice, and requires no ongoing effort once completed for the day.

Linsin explores why trying hard to stay calm often backfires, creating tension rather than relieving it, and instead recommends visualization as a proven method for building genuine, effortless composure.
